subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - North America
subtitle: Physical features, climates, people, resources, and sustainability across North America.
description: A source-faithful revision pack on North America as a world region. It covers major landforms, climate zones, population patterns, resources, migration, trade, urbanization, human-environment interaction, and case studies such as the Mississippi River, Colorado River Basin, Mexico City, the Arctic, and the Caribbean.

data.targetWord: an area that shares common features, such as physical, cultural, economic, or political features

examples.en-US: The Great Plains is a physical and farming region of North America.

data.targetWord: the natural surroundings of a place, including land, water, climate, plants, animals, and ecosystems

examples.en-US: The Arctic environment is cold, icy, and fragile.

data.targetWord: the usual weather patterns of a place over a long period of time

examples.en-US: Southern Florida has a warm, humid climate.

data.targetWord: the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere, such as rain, wind, heat, or snow

examples.en-US: A thunderstorm in Texas is weather, not climate.

data.targetWord: the number of people living in a place

examples.en-US: Mexico City has a very large population.

data.targetWord: how crowded a place is, usually measured as people per square mile or square kilometer

examples.en-US: Manhattan has high population density, while northern Canada has low population density.

data.targetWord: something from the environment that people use

examples.en-US: Oil, forests, fresh water, soil, fish, and minerals are resources.

data.targetWord: a useful material or feature found in nature

examples.en-US: Timber from Canadian forests is a natural resource.

data.targetWord: a resource that can be replaced naturally if it is managed carefully

examples.en-US: Wind energy, solar energy, forests, and fish can be renewable resources.

data.targetWord: a resource that forms very slowly and can run out

examples.en-US: Oil, coal, and natural gas are nonrenewable resources.

data.targetWord: the movement of people from one place to another to live

examples.en-US: People moving from rural areas to cities is migration.

data.targetWord: moving into a country to live

examples.en-US: A family moving from another country to Canada is immigration.

data.targetWord: leaving a country to live somewhere else

examples.en-US: A person leaving Mexico to live abroad is emigration.

data.targetWord: using resources in a way that meets present needs without damaging the future

examples.en-US: Protecting water supplies while farming is a sustainability goal.

data.targetWord: the growth of towns and cities as more people live and work there

examples.en-US: The growth of Toronto, Los Angeles, and Mexico City is part of urbanization.

data.targetWord: the first peoples of a place and their descendants, with diverse cultures, languages, histories, and lands

examples.en-US: Inuit, Navajo, Haudenosaunee, Maya, and many other Indigenous peoples live in North America.

data.targetWord: a high boundary that separates river systems flowing toward different oceans

examples.en-US: The Rocky Mountains form a major continental divide.

data.targetWord: an area of land where water drains into the same river, lake, or ocean

examples.en-US: The Mississippi River watershed drains a huge part of the United States.

data.targetWord: a large natural region with similar climate, plants, and animals

examples.en-US: Tundra, desert, grassland, and forest are biomes found in North America.

data.targetWord: buying, selling, and exchanging goods and services

examples.en-US: Canada, the United States, and Mexico trade cars, food, energy, and technology.

data.targetWord: basic systems that help communities function, such as roads, bridges, ports, power lines, and water systems

examples.en-US: Highways and railroads connect farms, factories, and cities.

data.targetWord: a dry area on the side of a mountain away from moist winds

examples.en-US: Mountain ranges can create rain shadows that make one side much drier.

data.targetWord: a long mountain system running through western North America

examples.en-US: The Rocky Mountains affect climate, rivers, transportation, tourism, and mining.

data.targetWord: older, lower mountains in eastern North America

examples.en-US: The Appalachian Mountains are lower and older than the Rocky Mountains.

data.targetWord: broad grasslands in central North America that are important for farming and ranching

examples.en-US: The Great Plains support wheat, corn, soybeans, and cattle ranching.

data.targetWord: an ancient rocky region with forests, lakes, and minerals

examples.en-US: The Canadian Shield has minerals, forests, lakes, and low population density in many areas.

data.targetWord: the five large lakes named Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario

examples.en-US: The Great Lakes support shipping, fresh water, fishing, and cities.

data.targetWord: one of the largest river systems in the world, connecting farms, cities, wetlands, and ports

examples.en-US: Barges on the Mississippi River move grain, fuel, and other goods.

data.targetWord: the river that links the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean

examples.en-US: Toronto and Montreal are connected to the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence River system.

data.targetWord: a river that forms part of the border between the United States and Mexico

examples.en-US: The Rio Grande is an important border and water feature.

data.targetWord: a dry-region river basin that supplies water to cities, farms, dams, recreation, and ecosystems

examples.en-US: The Colorado River Basin needs careful water management because demand can be greater than supply.

data.targetWord: one of North America's largest urban areas, located in a highland basin with major opportunities and planning challenges

examples.en-US: Mexico City's basin location affects air movement, water drainage, and city planning.

data.targetWord: Greenland, northern Canada, Alaska, and nearby Arctic islands, with cold environments and Indigenous communities

examples.en-US: Arctic North America has tundra, sea ice, permafrost, and long seasonal changes in daylight.

data.targetWord: island nations and territories around the Caribbean Sea, shaped by oceans, tourism, trade, hurricanes, and cultural diversity

examples.en-US: Caribbean communities often plan for hurricanes, coastal flooding, tourism pressure, and reef protection.

data.targetWord: a wet coastal ecosystem that can provide wildlife habitat and help reduce storm impacts

examples.en-US: Wetlands near the mouth of the Mississippi River help protect coasts and provide wildlife habitat.

data.targetWord: ground that stays frozen for a long time and can become unstable when it melts

examples.en-US: Melting permafrost can damage buildings, roads, and other infrastructure in Arctic areas.

data.targetWord: a powerful tropical storm that can bring strong winds, heavy rain, storm surge, flooding, and damage

examples.en-US: Hurricanes affect parts of the Caribbean, Gulf Coast, Atlantic Coast, and Central America.

data.targetWord: a rise of seawater pushed onto land by a storm, which can flood coastal areas

examples.en-US: Storm surge is one reason hurricanes are dangerous for island and coastal communities.

data.targetWord: a large uncontrolled fire that can threaten forests, homes, air quality, and wildlife

examples.en-US: Wildfires are a major sustainability challenge in parts of the western United States, western Canada, and Mexico.

data.targetWord: the ways people affect the environment and the ways the environment affects people

examples.en-US: Building dams, farming grasslands, protecting wetlands, and adapting to drought are examples of human-environment interaction.

data.hint: It can be physical, cultural, economic, or political.

data.sentence: ____ is the usual weather pattern of a place over a long period of time.
data.hint: It is not just today's condition.

data.sentence: A thunderstorm in Texas is an example of ____ rather than climate.
data.hint: It describes a short-term atmospheric condition.

data.sentence: The ____ River links the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean.
data.hint: It is important to eastern Canada and Great Lakes shipping.

data.sentence: The ____ Mountains run through western North America and form a major continental divide.
data.hint: This mountain system is in the west.

data.sentence: ____ measures how crowded a place is by comparing people with area.
data.hint: It is different from total population.

data.sentence: Oil, coal, and natural gas are ____ resources because they form slowly and can run out.
data.hint: They cannot be replaced quickly on a human timescale.

data.sentence: Using resources carefully so people today and in the future can meet their needs is called ____.
data.hint: It involves long-term planning.

data.sentence: The movement of people from one place to another to live is called ____.
data.hint: It can happen within countries or across borders.

data.sentence: The growth of towns and cities is called ____.
data.hint: It includes the growth of cities such as Toronto, Los Angeles, and Mexico City.

data.sentence: The three largest countries in North America by land area are Canada, the United States, and ____.
data.hint: This country links the United States to Central America.

data.sentence: The ____ is associated with sea ice, tundra, permafrost, and long seasonal changes in daylight.
data.hint: It lies north of Canada and Greenland.

data.sentence: Many Caribbean islands must plan for ____ because warm ocean storms can bring wind, flooding, and storm surge.
data.hint: These storms affect the Caribbean, Gulf Coast, and Atlantic Coast.

data.sentence: Water management is especially important in the ____ River Basin because it serves cities, farms, dams, recreation, and ecosystems in a dry region.
data.hint: This river is important in the dry Southwest.

data.sentence: The ____ River system supports transportation, farming, cities, wetlands, and ports in central North America.
data.hint: Cities such as St. Louis, Memphis, Baton Rouge, and New Orleans developed along it.

data.sentence: Mountain ranges can block moist air and create a dry ____ effect on the leeward side.
data.hint: It explains why one side of a mountain may be much drier.

data.sentence: Geographers should not describe the Arctic as empty because it is home to communities, ecosystems, and ____ knowledge.
data.hint: The source names Inuit and other groups as examples.

data.sentence: Mexico City's location in a highland ____ affects air movement, water drainage, and city planning.
data.hint: Mountains around the city can trap air pollution.

data.sentence: Canada, the United States, and Mexico are strongly connected through ____ involving cars, food, energy, and technology.
data.hint: Goods can cross borders several times before becoming finished products.

data.sentence: Healthy coral reefs and ____ can reduce wave energy and support fishing and tourism in coastal areas.
data.hint: The source links them to Caribbean sustainability.

data.title: How Physical Geography Can Shape a City
data.instruction: Put the cause-and-effect chain in the correct order.
items: A physical feature such as a natural harbor creates an opportunity.
The feature supports resources or transportation.
People settle nearby because trade, water, food, or jobs are available.
Businesses and workers arrive as economic activity grows.
The city expands and needs more infrastructure.
New challenges appear, such as traffic, pollution, housing demand, or water stress.

data.title: Colorado River Water Management
data.instruction: Order the steps from growing demand to more sustainable responses.
items: Cities, farms, dams, recreation, and ecosystems all need Colorado River water.
Demand can become higher than the river can reliably supply.
Drought and reduced snowpack can make river flow less dependable.
Communities must decide how to share limited water fairly.
Solutions such as drip irrigation, leak repairs, water reuse, and water-sharing agreements reduce pressure.
Protecting river habitats helps make the system more sustainable.

data.title: Preparing for a Caribbean Hurricane
data.instruction: Put these preparedness steps in a sensible order.
items: Weather monitoring identifies a developing tropical storm.
Public warning systems alert people in coastal and island communities.
Emergency shelters and evacuation routes are prepared.
Buildings, ports, power systems, and roads are secured where possible.
The hurricane brings wind, rain, storm surge, and possible flooding.
Recovery planning repairs damage and improves resilience for future storms.

data.title: North America Geography and Change
data.instruction: Put these broad geographic change patterns in chronological order.
items: Indigenous peoples develop diverse ways of life across forests, plains, deserts, mountains, Arctic coasts, and islands.
European colonization reshapes land use, settlement, trade, languages, and power from the 1500s onward.
Forced migration through slavery has deep human and cultural impacts, especially in plantation and port regions.
Railroads, canals, mining, farming expansion, and industrial cities transform landscapes in the 1800s.
Urbanization, highways, dams, suburbs, factories, and oil use grow quickly in the 1900s.
Technology, global trade, climate concerns, migration, and sustainability planning shape the region today.
